lesson.title: Counter: One Line to Tally Anything
lesson.summary: collections.Counter is a dict subclass purpose-built for counting hashable items, automatically tallying an iterable's contents and offering a most_common method, while safely returning 0 rather than an error for items it has never seen.
lesson.body:
You have already learned to count things with a plain dictionary, typically by writing something like counts[item] = counts.get(item, 0) + 1, or by reaching for defaultdict(int) to avoid the manual existence check. Counter, also from the collections module, exists because counting is such a common task that Python's standard library gives it a dedicated tool rather than making you rebuild that same few lines every time.

Pass any iterable of hashable items into Counter and it counts every occurrence for you in a single step, no loop required on your part. The result behaves like a dictionary mapping each distinct item to how many times it appeared, plus a few extras. The most useful extra is most_common(n), which returns the n most frequent items as a list of (item, count) tuples, sorted from most frequent to least. Counter also has a quietly important safety behavior: looking up a key that was never counted returns 0 instead of raising a KeyError, similar in spirit to defaultdict(int), but with one real difference, accessing a missing key in a Counter does not add that key to the Counter the way defaultdict would. It just answers 0 and moves on.

```python
from collections import Counter

votes = ["red", "blue", "red", "green", "blue", "red"]
tally = Counter(votes)
print(tally)
print(tally["red"])
print(tally["purple"])
print(tally.most_common(2))
```

Counter(votes) scans the list once: red appears 3 times, blue appears 2 times, green appears 1 time. Its printed form lists items from most common to least, so the output begins:

```
Counter({'red': 3, 'blue': 2, 'green': 1})
3
0
[('red', 3), ('blue', 2)]
```

tally["red"] correctly returns 3. tally["purple"], a color that never appeared in votes, returns 0 rather than crashing the program, which is exactly the behavior you want when you are not sure in advance whether an item was ever seen. most_common(2) hands back the two most frequent entries as tuples, ready to unpack in a for loop if you need the winner and runner-up of an election, the two most common words in a document, or the busiest two hours in a log file. Counter is the tool to reach for the moment your task description contains the word tally, frequency, or count, it turns what used to be a several-line loop into a single constructor call.
